📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that an international consortium has created personalized biophysical “digital brain twins” for 6,986 individuals across 16 countries to uncover how aging, neurodegenerative diseases, and environmental conditions shape neural dynamics. The computational models simulate excitation-inhibition balance across 90 connected brain regions, revealing distinct mechanistic signatures for Alzheimer’s disease, frontotemporal degeneration, and environmental exposures ranging from air pollution to democratic governance.

Standard magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) provides an invaluable window into the living human brain, yet it records only indirect proxies of neural activity, typically relying on group averages that obscure individual variation and say little about the underlying cellular mechanisms driving those signals.

Now, an international research team led by corresponding author Dr. Agustín Ibáñez (Scientific Director of BrainLat at Universidad Adolfo Ibáñez, strategic director of core scientific assets at the BarcelonaBeta Brain Research Center, and faculty at the Global Brain Health Institute at Trinity College Dublin) and first author Dr. Rubén Herzog (BrainLat and Distinguished Professor at the University of the Balearic Islands) has transformed static brain scans into dynamic, personalized virtual laboratories.

Published today in Nature Biomedical Engineering, the study introduces biophysical “digital brain twins” constructed from resting-state functional MRI (fMRI) scans of 6,986 individuals spanning ages 18 to 100 across 16 countries.

Rather than treating brain scans as passive statistical snapshots, biophysical brain twins apply mathematical equations grounded in neurobiology to simulate how populations of excitatory and inhibitory neurons interact across 90 connected brain regions.

Sources indicate that for each participant, the investigators tuned their computational model until its simulated fMRI output closely matched the individual’s actual resting-state brain recordings. Independent validation showed that model-derived regional excitability closely correlated with structural grey matter volume, confirming that the virtual simulations capture real biological architecture.

“Every brain ages in a different context. Our biophysical twins help us study how the variations in our biology and the social and environmental conditions of our lives relate to brain function,” explained Ibáñez. “The importance of biophysical brain twins is that they connect what brain scans record with the underlying processes that could produce those signals. Each twin acts as a personalised virtual laboratory: researchers can adjust how its neural populations interact and examine how those changes affect the whole brain. This opens a route from observing differences to testing possible explanations, mechanisms, potential treatments and interventions.”.

It has been revealed that “MRI records indirect measures of neural activity. Biophysical twins let us simulate the neural processes that might generate those signals and explore why they differ from person to person,” added Herzog.

Applying these nearly 7,000 personalized models across diverse clinical cohorts exposed clear mechanistic boundaries between normal aging and dementia:.

To overcome the historical divide between neuroimaging and real-world lived context, the team linked individual brain models with macro-level environmental indicators across 10 domains alongside personal socioeconomic histories.

Robust associations emerged in seven of the ten environmental domains, most prominently in indicators measuring democratic conditions (free choices, civic participation, political representation, and rule of law), soil and water quality, and air pollution. Complementary analyses of individual life circumstances further linked brain dynamics to healthcare access, childhood experiences, and financial stability. These relationships persisted even after controlling for age, sex, clinical diagnosis, country, and MRI scanner hardware.

By releasing their open-source code and model parameters, the authors have established a global testbed for in silico experimentation. Future studies can overlay neurotransmitter receptor maps onto these digital twins—simulating how targeted modulation of glutamate (excitatory) or GABA (inhibitory) signaling, or public health improvements in air quality and healthcare access, might shift an aging brain back toward healthy functional patterns.

What is a biophysical “digital brain twin”?

A digital brain twin is a personalized computer simulation built from an individual’s fMRI scan using biological equations. By modeling how 90 connected brain regions interact, it allows researchers to estimate underlying cellular processes, such as the balance between signals that excite or inhibit neurons—and test virtual treatments safely on a computer.

How do brain dynamics differ between normal aging and dementia?

In the study of nearly 7,000 people, normal aging primarily changed how regularly or unpredictably brain activity fluctuated over time. In contrast, Alzheimer’s disease and frontotemporal degeneration disrupted overall activity levels, variability, and the balance between excitatory and inhibitory brain signals all at once.

Can environmental and social conditions really affect how the brain functions?

According to recent reports, yes. Even after accounting for age, sex, diagnosis, and scanner differences, researchers found that environmental factors, especially democratic conditions, soil and water quality, air pollution, healthcare access, and financial circumstances, were measurably linked to underlying simulated brain dynamics.

Biophysical brain twins map the phenotype–expotype architecture of ageing and dementia.

Biophysical whole-brain models may reveal causal links between neural dynamics and biological–environmental variation, yet no framework has explained how these factors become embedded in mechanistic dynamics.

Here we develop individualized biophysical digital twins mechanistically linked to phenotypes and expotypes (that is, combinations of exposomal influences) leveraging resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging data (n = 6,986, 16 countries) of healthy controls and participants with mild cognitive impairment, Alzheimer’s disease and frontotemporal dementia.

Personalized twins improved goodness-of-fit over group-level models. They reproduced structure–function coupling between regional excitability and brain volume, captured age, sex and neurodegeneration, and encoded 68 expotypes.

According to recent reports, associations remained robust after controlling for demographics, data quality, model fit and scanner/site, with the strongest effects for social and physical (pollution) exposomes. We release an open resource (empirical data, code, >3 million simulations) for future research.

These findings ground phenotypic–exposomic variation in individualized biophysical twins, enabling in silico testing of mechanisms and potential model-informed interventions.

📅 19 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2634 w)

General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

"Mind-blowing" Alzheimer’s breakthrough: Two hours of sleep restored without clearing brain plaques

📅 19 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2634 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Scientists have discovered an unexpected reason why Alzheimer's disease disrupts sleep, and their findings suggest that the problem may be reversible.
  • Recent findings suggest that the surprising discovery points to an overlooked culprit: the brain's own immune cells.
  • It has been revealed that researchers at the University of Kentucky found that temporarily eliminating most of these immune cells allowed the mice to sleep longer and spend more time in the deep, restorative stages of sleep.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scientists have discovered an unexpected reason why Alzheimer's disease disrupts sleep, and their findings suggest that the problem may be reversible. In experiments involving mice with Alzheimer's-like brain changes, researchers restored more than two hours of sleep per day without removing the amyloid plaques associated with the disease.

Recent findings suggest that the surprising discovery points to an overlooked culprit: the brain's own immune cells. Rather than simply protecting the brain from damage, these cells can trigger inflammation that interferes with healthy sleep.

It has been revealed that researchers at the University of Kentucky found that temporarily eliminating most of these immune cells allowed the mice to sleep longer and spend more time in the deep, restorative stages of sleep. The results suggest a potential new approach to treating one of the most disruptive symptoms of Alzheimer's disease.

According to recent reports, the findings, published in the journal Alzheimer's & Dementia, were reported by a team led by Shannon L. Macauley, Ph.D., an associate professor of physiology at the University of Kentucky College of Medicine, and first author Nicholas J. Constantino, Ph.D., a recent doctoral graduate.

Macauley described the discovery as "paradigm-shifting" because it challenges the prevailing understanding of why people with Alzheimer's often experience severe sleep problems.

How the Brain's Immune System Can Disrupt Sleep.

Recent findings suggest that to understand what the researchers uncovered, imagine a small fire breaking out in a kitchen. Instead of containing the flames, the building's sprinkler system activates everywhere, flooding the entire house and causing widespread damage.

Something similar may happen in the brain during Alzheimer's disease.

Amyloid plaques are deposits of sticky protein fragments that accumulate between nerve cells. They are one of the characteristic features of Alzheimer's and have long been investigated for their role in the disease.

Sources indicate that the brain also contains specialized immune cells known as microglia. These cells normally protect the nervous system by removing debris, responding to injuries, and helping maintain a healthy environment for neurons.

Sources indicate that however, when microglia detect amyloid plaques, their defensive response can become excessive. Instead of simply addressing the threat, they release inflammatory signals that may interfere with normal brain activity.

Scientists have traditionally linked sleep problems in Alzheimer's primarily to damaged neurons or the accumulation of amyloid plaques. The latest findings suggest that the immune system's reaction to those plaques plays a major role.

Sources indicate that "Basically, we showed that it is not the plaques themselves, or solely dysfunctional neurons, that cause sleep loss but actually microglia," stated Macauley. "Microglia are immune cells that, when they respond to plaques, kick off this elaborate cascade of inflammation, as if the microglia are partying all night, and keeping the brain awake.".

In other words, the brain's response to Alzheimer's pathology may create additional problems beyond those caused by the plaques themselves. The researchers compared this widespread reaction to a "whole house response," in which a defense mechanism ends up causing more disruption than expected.

Tracking Alzheimer's Sleep Changes Inside the Brain.

To investigate the connection between microglia and sleep, the scientists studied two groups of mice. One group was genetically predisposed to develop amyloid plaques, while the other consisted of normal "wild-type" mice that experienced typical aging.

The researchers examined the animals at two ages: six months, when plaques first appeared in the genetically modified mice, and 18 months, when the disease model highlighted more advanced pathology.

Comparing these groups helped the scientists distinguish changes associated with Alzheimer's pathology from those that naturally occur as the brain ages.

The team used several advanced technologies to measure sleep and examine what was happening inside the brain.

Each mouse was fitted with a small device that recorded electroencephalography (EEG) and electromyography (EMG).

Sources indicate that EEG measures the brain's electrical activity, including the patterns and rhythms produced when networks of neurons communicate. These electrical signals change depending on whether the brain is awake, dreaming or experiencing deep sleep.

According to recent reports, EMG measures electrical activity in muscles. Combining the two techniques allowed researchers to identify different sleep stages and determine how long the animals remained in each one.

The scientists also wanted to visualize the relationship between amyloid plaques and immune cells throughout the brain.

Recent findings suggest that for this, they used light-sheet microscopy, an imaging technique that makes biological tissue transparent and illuminates it with a thin layer of laser light. The resulting images can be assembled into detailed three-dimensional maps, allowing scientists to examine structures that would otherwise be difficult to see.

This approach revealed the distribution of plaques and microglia across the brain, helping researchers understand where immune cells were responding to Alzheimer's pathology.

Scientists Temporarily Remove 87% of Brain Immune Cells.

To determine whether microglia were actually responsible for disrupted sleep, the team conducted an experiment designed to temporarily eliminate most of these cells.

The researchers administered a drug called Pexidartinib (PLX3397), which was originally developed for cancer research. It blocks a cellular signal that microglia depend on for survival.

After the mice received the medication in their food for 14 days, approximately 87% of their microglia had been depleted.

This allowed the scientists to test whether sleep would improve when the cells driving the inflammatory response were largely absent.

The researchers also performed a detailed analysis of the animals' brain activity using a mathematical method called Fitting Oscillations and One Over Frequency (FOOOF).

This technique separates electrical signals into periodic activity (the rhythmic waves we usually think of as brain waves) and aperiodic activity (the background electrical noise).

By examining these different components, the team could identify changes in how the brain was functioning, including whether it remained unusually active during periods when it should have been resting.

The process is somewhat like monitoring a car engine to determine whether it continues running at high speed even when the vehicle is supposed to be idle.

A Surprising Discovery About Alzheimer's Brain Plaques.

Macauley called the results "mind-blowing and unexpected.".

One of the most surprising findings was that sleep problems did not continue worsening as amyloid plaques accumulated.

The researchers initially expected that increasing plaque buildup would lead to progressively more severe sleep disturbances. Instead, the mice developed substantial sleep problems relatively early, and those problems remained largely unchanged even as plaque levels increased dramatically.

Sources indicate that "I expected that as plaque burden became more severe, sleep disruption would also worsen," said Constantino. "The disruptions in sleep and cortical EEG activity that occur at 6 months, when plaques first emerge, did not worsen by 18 months, despite more than double the amount of plaque burden.".

The team described this pattern as a ceiling effect. Essentially, sleep disruption appeared to reach a certain level early in the disease process rather than increasing in direct proportion to the amount of amyloid in the brain.

This suggests that the initial inflammatory response triggered by plaques may be particularly important. Once microglia become activated and disrupt sleep, additional plaque accumulation may not necessarily produce an equivalent increase in sleep loss.

The discovery offers an key clue as to why sleep disturbances can emerge relatively early in Alzheimer's disease.

Alzheimer's Disrupts a Different Type of Sleep Than Normal Aging.

The study also revealed a notable difference between sleep changes caused by normal aging and those associated with Alzheimer's pathology.

In a recent development, sleep is not a single, uniform state. Throughout the night, the brain moves through several stages that perform different functions.

Rapid eye movement (REM) sleep is strongly associated with vivid dreaming and plays an vital role in processing memories. The researchers found that normal aging primarily reduced this type of sleep.

Alzheimer's pathology, however, had a different effect. It selectively disrupted non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep, which includes the deepest and most physically restorative stages of sleep.

Sources indicate that during NREM sleep, the brain performs essential maintenance functions that support learning, memory, and recovery. Deep sleep is also associated with processes that help clear metabolic waste products from the brain.

"That restorative sleep is super crucial for physical repair, learning and memory and washing out the toxins of the day," Macauley said.

Losing this important stage of sleep could have consequences beyond daytime fatigue.

Because healthy sleep helps maintain the brain's internal environment, disruptions may interfere with processes that normally remove potentially harmful waste. Researchers suspect this could contribute to a self-reinforcing cycle in which Alzheimer's pathology disturbs sleep, and inadequate sleep may further aggravate the disease.

Breaking that cycle could therefore become an important treatment strategy.

More Than Two Hours of Sleep Restored Without Removing Plaques.

The most striking result emerged after the researchers temporarily removed most of the microglia from the brains of mice with Alzheimer's-like pathology.

The animals gained more than two hours of sleep per day.

They also experienced longer periods of restorative NREM sleep, giving them more opportunities to transition naturally into REM sleep, which is important for memory formation.

Even more surprisingly, these improvements occurred without any reduction in amyloid plaque levels.

The plaques were still present, but the mice were sleeping substantially better.

This finding provides evidence that the inflammatory response driven by microglia contributes directly to sleep disruption and that suppressing this response can reverse at least some of the associated sleep problems.

It also suggests that researchers may not need to eliminate amyloid plaques to improve sleep in Alzheimer's disease.

In a recent development, although these findings are promising, the experiments were conducted in mice, and the same benefits have not yet been demonstrated in people. Temporarily removing most of the brain's immune cells is also not an established or practical treatment for Alzheimer's patients.

The researchers are now interested in whether the beneficial effects can be reproduced by adjusting microglial activity rather than eliminating the cells themselves.

If such an approach eventually proves successful in humans, it could provide a way to improve sleep and potentially reduce some of the additional stress that poor sleep places on the brain.

The Research Team Behind the Discovery.

The work was conducted in Macauley's laboratory in the Department of Physiology at the University of Kentucky's Sanders-Brown Center on Aging.

Macauley credits the achievement to a "beautiful partnership" with students and researchers who were willing to challenge established ideas about Alzheimer's disease.

"I love people who take initiative, find their passion, are curious, and keep pushing to find an answer," Macauley noted.

She encourages members of her laboratory to be "calculated risk-takers," emphasizing that meaningful discoveries often require scientists to investigate possibilities that may initially seem unlikely.

A quote from hockey legend Wayne Gretzky hangs in her office: "You miss 100% of the shots you don't take.".

Constantino, who recently completed his doctorate at the university, said the laboratory's collaborative environment encouraged him to pursue questions that crossed traditional scientific disciplines.

In a recent development, "Dr. Macauley has also taught me to embrace uncertainty and failure as part of the scientific process," Constantino remarked. "Some of the most interesting studies I have been a part of emerged because our original hypothesis was wrong.".

Macauley reinforces this mindset with a simple instruction to her team: "Follow the data, ask better questions, and figure out what is actually happening.".

That approach helped the researchers move beyond the traditional emphasis on neurons and amyloid plaques to examine the broader role of the brain's immune system.

Could Existing Medications Help Restore Sleep in Alzheimer's?

The research team is now exploring ways to translate these findings into treatments and diagnostic tools that could eventually benefit people with Alzheimer's disease.

One promising direction involves calming overactive microglia without removing them.

Sources indicate that because microglia perform essential protective functions, eliminating them is not an ideal long-term strategy. Instead, the researchers hope to modify how these immune cells respond to amyloid plaques and regulate inflammation.

The laboratory is investigating existing medications, including the diabetes drug Metformin and the anti-seizure medication Stiripentol.

These drugs are being studied for their potential to alter how microglia produce and use energy, a process known as cellular metabolism. Changing that energy use could potentially reduce excessive immune activation and its harmful effects on sleep.

The hope is to prevent the brain's inflammatory response from becoming so intense that it disrupts normal sleep activity.

Researchers are particularly interested in whether intervention during the earlier stages of Alzheimer's could improve sleep and quality of life before substantial memory loss develops.

"If we can target that process, it might help with quality of life, attention, cognition and confusion," Macauley noted.

The proposed drug strategies remain experimental for this purpose, and additional research will be necessary to determine whether they can safely produce similar benefits in humans.

A Simpler Way to Detect Early Alzheimer's Changes.

Beyond identifying a potential treatment target, the study uncovered electrical activity patterns that may help distinguish Alzheimer's pathology from normal brain aging.

The researchers believe these patterns could eventually make EEG a useful tool for detecting and monitoring changes associated with Alzheimer's disease.

Unlike more expensive imaging procedures, EEG records electrical signals through electrodes placed on the scalp. It is relatively affordable, does not require surgery, and can be repeated to follow changes over time.

The team envisions EEG becoming a "readily accessible, affordable and longitudinal biomarker of Alzheimer's disease.".

A biomarker is a measurable biological sign that provides information about a person's health or a particular disease. A longitudinal biomarker can be tracked repeatedly to monitor how a condition develops or changes.

"Portable EEG systems could allow us to monitor people in their home environments and potentially screen for changes associated with an Alzheimer's disease, without the initial need for expensive or invasive tests," Macauley mentioned.

If future human studies confirm the usefulness of these electrical signatures, portable EEG devices might eventually help doctors identify people who need additional testing.

This could be particularly valuable in rural communities across Kentucky, where patients sometimes must travel long distances to reach specialized medical centers.

Instead of requiring every potentially at-risk patient to undergo advanced testing immediately, local clinics might use simpler monitoring tools to identify individuals who would benefit from further evaluation.

Although this application still requires validation, it offers a possible path toward more accessible Alzheimer's screening and monitoring.

Ultimately, the study suggests that treating Alzheimer's may require looking beyond the plaques themselves and examining how the brain responds to them.

By identifying the immune cells responsible for much of the sleep disruption in their mouse models, the University of Kentucky researchers have uncovered a potential way to restore an essential brain function without first removing the underlying amyloid deposits.

The next challenge is determining whether calming these cells can deliver similar benefits in people, potentially improving sleep, cognition and quality of life long before the most severe symptoms of Alzheimer's develop.

Tech Report: The Brain Creates Body Ownership Before Touch Occurs

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (948 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Neurosciencenews

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that researchers have mapped the exact millisecond-by-millisecond sequence of brain activity that creates the feeling that a hand belongs to our own body.
  • We effortlessly take for granted that our hands, arms, and limbs belong to us.
  • While prior neuroimaging studies identified the general brain regions involved in self-perception, the exact temporal choreography, when each region activates and how signals cascade across the cortex, has remained elusive.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that researchers have mapped the exact millisecond-by-millisecond sequence of brain activity that creates the feeling that a hand belongs to our own body. The magnetoencephalography (MEG) study reveals three distinct neural phases, beginning even before physical touch occurs, and explains why right-hemisphere strokes frequently cause patients to disown their left arm.

We effortlessly take for granted that our hands, arms, and limbs belong to us. Yet this seamless sense of body ownership is an active perceptual construction, one that requires the brain to continuously merge visual, tactile, and spatial signals in real time, and one that can shatter dramatically following neurological injury.

While prior neuroimaging studies identified the general brain regions involved in self-perception, the exact temporal choreography, when each region activates and how signals cascade across the cortex, has remained elusive.

Now, in a study published in Nature Communications, neuroscientists at Karolinska Institutet led by Professor Henrik Ehrsson (Department of Neuroscience) and co-author Professor Daniel Lundqvist (Department of Clinical Neuroscience) have charted the birth of body ownership millisecond by millisecond.

To capture how the brain constructs the feeling that a limb is its own, the team recruited 45 healthy volunteers for a precision robotic version of the classic rubber hand illusion.

Participants watched a lifelike artificial hand resting in front of them while their real left hand remained hidden behind a screen. Two robotic arms delivered brief, synchronized touches to both the visible rubber hand and the concealed real hand, while high-speed magnetoencephalography (MEG) recorded whole-brain magnetic fields. By comparing synchronized touches (which trigger the illusion that the rubber hand is part of one’s body) against asynchronous touches and real-hand control conditions, the researchers isolated the neural signature of body ownership across the 28 participants who vividly experienced the illusion.

Reconstructing brain activity every four milliseconds produced a real-time movie of self-perception unfolding across three distinct phases:.

“We know quite a lot about which areas of the brain are involved in the sense that the body is our own, but considerably less about when different areas become active and how they interact. We have now been able to track how activity patterns in the brain develop over time,” explained Ehrsson.

“The fact that the activity began even before the hand was touched shows that the brain’s expectations of what we are going to feel are closely linked to the conscious experience of the body as our own,” added Lundqvist. “This study shows when, in what order, and how different brain regions help combine information from different senses into a unified experience of our own body.”.

Recent findings suggest that notably, during the first two phases of the sequence, neural activity was confined almost entirely to the right hemisphere. This lateralized timing aligns strikingly with clinical neurology: following a stroke, patients who experience somatoparaphrenia, the disturbing condition in which a limb no longer feels like part of one’s own body, almost always disown their left arm after damage to the right hemisphere.

“When stroke patients lose the sense that an arm belongs to them, it is usually the left arm that is affected, following damage to the right hemisphere of the brain,” Ehrsson noted. “In future studies, we want to compare patterns of brain activity associated with the right and left hands to better understand the different roles of the brain’s hemispheres. We also want to collaborate with stroke researchers to investigate this phenomenon in patients.”.

How does the brain create the feeling that your hand belongs to your body?

Karolinska Institutet researchers found that body ownership arises through a precise three-stage sequence of brain activity. It starts with predictive expectation before a hand is even touched, sweeps rapidly across the right frontal, parietal, and cerebellar regions, and finally engages the left hemisphere to unify sensory information.

Why did brain activity start before the hand was physically touched?

Industry observers note that seeing an object approach the hand triggers predictive brain activity based on what we expect to feel. This pre-touch expectation primes the brain to merge sight and touch into the conscious experience that the limb is our own.

How does this study help explain disturbed body perception after a stroke?

Because the first two critical stages of body ownership occur almost exclusively in the brain’s right hemisphere, damage to that side from a stroke disrupts the early multisensory integration needed to recognize the left arm, explaining why stroke patients frequently lose the sense that their left arm belongs to them.

Funding: The study was funded by the Swedish Research Council, the Göran Gustafsson Foundation, the Torsten Söderberg Foundation and the Swedish Brain Foundation. NatMEG receives support from the Knut and Alice Wallenberg Foundation. The researchers declare no conflicts of interest.

Spatiotemporal brain dynamics of limb ownership perception.

We experience our limbs as our own, but how does the brain generate this fundamental sense of body ownership?

Previous studies have relied mainly on fMRI or lesion mapping, providing a static view of the neural mechanisms underlying body ownership.

Using magnetoencephalography, robotically controlled visuotactile stimulation, and multivariate analysis across the rubber hand illusion, a real hand condition, and multiple control conditions, we identified source vector dissimilarity patterns reflecting ownership of the left arm.

Three phases of ownership-specific activity patterns emerged: (i) anticipatory patterns in medial frontal cortex, right posterior parietal cortex, and right posterior cerebellum before tactile stimulation; (ii) multisensory integration patterns in right dorsal and ventral premotor cortex, right posterior parietal cortex, and anterior cerebellum at 116–156 ms poststimulus; and (iii) later bilateral insular and left hemisphere patterns at 184–232 ms.

These findings provide a whole-brain, time-resolved map of activity patterns underlying body ownership, revealing its dynamic neural construction.

Psilocybin and Ketamine Break Rigid Habits to Improve Decision-Making

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that new neuroscience research reveals that both psilocybin and ketamine improve decision accuracy by helping the brain rely less on rigid, repetitive habits and more on real-time sensory cues.
  • For the roughly one in five Americans living with a mental health condition, frontline psychiatric medications have changed remarkably little since the 1950s.
  • It has been revealed that against this backdrop, psychedelic compounds, including classic serotonergic psychedelics like psilocybin and dissociative agents like ketamine, have sparked intense clinical excitement for their ability to produce rapid, durable improvements in mood, addiction, and post-traumatic stress disorder.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that new neuroscience research reveals that both psilocybin and ketamine improve decision accuracy by helping the brain rely less on rigid, repetitive habits and more on real-time sensory cues. The study highlights that rather than scrambling neural signaling, these compounds gently sculpt ongoing brain activity, trading a slight reduction in reaction speed for sharper, more flexible choices.

For the roughly one in five Americans living with a mental health condition, frontline psychiatric medications have changed remarkably little since the 1950s. Conventional antidepressants such as selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) often require weeks to take effect, demand chronic daily use, and fail to provide adequate relief for roughly 30% of patients with treatment-resistant depression.

It has been revealed that against this backdrop, psychedelic compounds, including classic serotonergic psychedelics like psilocybin and dissociative agents like ketamine, have sparked intense clinical excitement for their ability to produce rapid, durable improvements in mood, addiction, and post-traumatic stress disorder. Yet precisely how these drugs alter neural circuits to break entrenched patterns of negative thinking has remained poorly understood.

According to recent reports, now, in a study published in Science Advances, neuroscientists at Boston University led by assistant professor Dr. Benjamin Scott and associate professor Dr. Steve Ramirez have uncovered a shared pro-cognitive mechanism linking psilocybin and ketamine: both drugs weaken the brain’s reliance on automatic habits and heighten sensitivity to immediate sensory cues.

To test how psychedelics influence moment-to-moment decision-making, Scott, Ramirez, and colleagues trained mice on a perceptual task requiring the animals to use brief pulses of light to identify which of two ports contained a reward.

Sources indicate that untreated mice performed the task moderately well, but frequently fell into habitual traps—repeatedly returning to a previously rewarded location even when the light cues clearly signaled a change. Following administration of either psilocybin or ketamine, however, mice made significantly fewer errors. Rather than falling back on repetitive choice biases, treated animals anchored their decisions much more closely to real-time sensory information.

“These findings reveal how psychedelics reduce the reliance on habits and repetitive choices, which may explain part of their therapeutic effect,” explained Scott, a faculty member in Boston University’s Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences.

Although psilocybin acts primarily on serotonin receptors (such as 5-HT2A and 5-HT1A) while ketamine blocks glutamate NMDA receptors, their behavioral effects converged on sharper, less biased decision-making.

To observe what changed inside the brain, the researchers combined brain-wide genetic activity mapping with targeted neural recordings in the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), a prefrontal region essential for evaluating rewards, making decisions, and updating beliefs when rules change.

According to recent reports, remarkably, psilocybin did not erase or scramble existing task representations. Instead, core OFC activity patterns tracking sensory cues and choices remained largely intact, accompanied by widespread yet subtle adjustments across interconnected brain regions. According to the authors, this gentle sculpting of ongoing neural activity aligns closely with clinical observations that a person’s mindset and environment (“set and setting”) strongly shape the psychedelic experience.

The team also identified an important behavioral nuance: while mice made more accurate choices after receiving psilocybin or ketamine, they took longer to deliberate, revealing a classic speed-accuracy tradeoff. While slower deliberation can benefit reflective cognitive therapy, it underscores why activities demanding split-second reaction times, such as driving, are unsafe under the influence of these compounds.

Looking ahead, Scott and Ramirez plan to pinpoint the exact neural pathways responsible for breaking rigid habits, with the ultimate goal of developing targeted, next-generation therapies that unlock cognitive flexibility without hallucinogenic side effects.

How do psilocybin and ketamine improve decision-making in this study?

Boston University researchers found that both drugs help the brain pay closer attention to immediate sensory cues (like flashes of light) while reducing the tendency to fall back on repetitive habits, leading to significantly more accurate choices.

Do psychedelics scramble normal brain activity during a task?

Recent findings suggest that no. Recordings in the orbitofrontal cortex revealed that the brain’s core patterns for tracking cues and making decisions remained largely preserved. Instead of causing chaos, psilocybin induced widespread yet subtle shifts that gently sculpted how the brain updated its beliefs.

Were there any downsides to the improved decision accuracy?

Recent findings suggest that yes. Researchers observed a speed-accuracy tradeoff: while treated animals made fewer mistakes, they took longer to make their decisions, suggesting these compounds slow down reaction times even as they promote more deliberative thinking.

Psychedelics Shift Decision Strategies and Reconfigure Orbitofrontal Dynamics.

Psychedelics such as psilocybin and ketamine are attracting renewed attention as rapid-acting therapeutics, yet how they reshape cognitive computations remains poorly understood.

Industry observers note that to address this, we trained mice on a free-response perceptual decision-making task that disentangles bias-driven from sensory-guided strategies. Acute administration of psilocybin or ketamine slowed decision times while improving accuracy. Behavioral modeling combining drift diffusion and GLM-HMM approaches revealed that these effects were driven by increased decision thresholds and a shift toward sensory-engaged states.

Recent findings suggest that whole-brain c-Fos mapping identified modulation of distributed task-related networks, including the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC). Calcium imaging indicated that OFC population dynamics were reorganized under psychedelic conditions, with preserved task selectivity but altered temporal structure and shifted population correlations.

Together, these findings indicate that psychedelics shift decision-making toward greater reliance on sensory evidence while reshaping cortical population dynamics, providing a system-level account of their effects on perceptual decisions.

Rising Blood Sugar in Young Adults Hurts Midlife Brain Health

💡 Key Takeaways

  • While Type 2 diabetes has long been recognized as a risk factor for late-life dementia, cognitive impairment linked to blood sugar was historically thought to emerge primarily after age 65.
  • Now, a three-decade investigation published today in the Journal of the American Heart Association demonstrates that creeping elevations in fasting blood sugar starting in young adulthood can measurably undermine memory, processing speed, and executive function by middle age, even among individuals who never cross the diagnostic threshold into full-blown diabetes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A 30-year longitudinal study reveals that young adults whose fasting blood sugar gradually rises over decades face significantly worse cognitive health by midlife, even if they never develop Type 2 diabetes. Tracking nearly 3,000 adults from age 18 into their mid-50s, researchers found lower memory, processing speed, and executive function scores among those with rising glucose trajectories, alongside structural brain changes in participants who developed Type 2 diabetes.

Source: American Heart Association.

While Type 2 diabetes has long been recognized as a risk factor for late-life dementia, cognitive impairment linked to blood sugar was historically thought to emerge primarily after age 65.

Now, a three-decade investigation published today in the Journal of the American Heart Association demonstrates that creeping elevations in fasting blood sugar starting in young adulthood can measurably undermine memory, processing speed, and executive function by middle age, even among individuals who never cross the diagnostic threshold into full-blown diabetes.

Led by first author Dr. Regina Paradela (postdoctoral researcher at the University of São Paulo Medical School and neuroepidemiologist at the Global Brain Health Institute at UC San Francisco) and senior author Dr. Kristine Yaffe (director of the Center for Population Brain Health at UC San Francisco), the study tracked metabolic and cognitive trajectories across 2,808 participants in the landmark Coronary Artery Risk Development in Young Adults (CARDIA) cohort.

Recent findings suggest that enrolled between 1985 and 1986 at ages 18 to 30 across four U.S. cities, participants underwent repeated fasting blood glucose measurements over 30 years until reaching an average age of 55. At the 30-year mark, all participants completed comprehensive neuropsychological testing, and a subset of 605 participants underwent brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).

By mapping longitudinal glucose patterns across the 2,463 participants who remained free of Type 2 diabetes, the researchers identified three distinct metabolic trajectories:.

An additional 345 participants developed Type 2 diabetes (fasting glucose ≥126 mg/dL) during the 30-year follow-up.

Even after adjusting for demographic and lifestyle factors, both the increasing-glucose group and the Type 2 diabetes group performed significantly worse on tests of memory, processing speed, executive function, and global cognition compared with the lower-stable glucose group.

“The fact that increasing glucose levels were associated with poorer cognitive performance, even among people who had not developed Type 2 diabetes during the 30-year study, is very important,” explained Paradela. “This suggests that changes in glucose metabolism may be relevant to brain health earlier in adulthood than we typically think about.”.

Furthermore, MRI scans revealed tangible anatomical footprints among participants who developed Type 2 diabetes, who exhibited less total gray matter and more abnormal white matter tissue, markers closely tied to accelerated brain aging and cognitive decline.

“Future research should evaluate whether monitoring and managing increasing glucose levels earlier in adulthood can prevent or delay cognitive decline and structural brain changes,” said senior author Yaffe.

Commenting on the study, Dr. Elisabeth Marsh, professor of neurology at The Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine and chair of the writing group for the American Heart Association’s 2026 scientific statement Brain Health Across the Life Span, emphasized the value of early vascular and metabolic care: “The American Heart Association’s Life’s Essential 8 offers steps to improve heart and brain health and support cognitive well-being at every stage of life.”.

Can rising blood sugar harm brain health even if you don’t have diabetes?

Yes. Over a 30-year study, young adults whose fasting blood sugar gradually increased into the prediabetic range (110–115 mg/dL) scored significantly worse on midlife tests of memory, processing speed, and executive function than peers whose blood sugar remained low and stable, even though they never developed Type 2 diabetes.

What structural brain changes were seen in participants who developed Type 2 diabetes?

MRI brain scans revealed that adults who developed Type 2 diabetes by their mid-50s had less total gray matter volume and more abnormal white matter tissue compared to those who maintained lower-stable blood sugar levels from young adulthood.

When should adults start paying attention to blood sugar for brain protection?

Researchers note that changes in glucose metabolism begin affecting cognitive performance much earlier than age 65. Monitoring and managing blood sugar trajectories starting in young adulthood, using healthy nutrition, physical activity, and cardiovascular risk control, may help protect midlife and late-life brain health.

Funding: Co-authors, disclosures and funding sources are listed in the manuscript.

Trajectories of Fasting Blood Glucose and Brain Health in Middle Age.

Research on associations between long‐term fasting blood glucose (FBG) trajectories and brain health in early adulthood is limited. We investigated associations of FBG trajectories with cognition and brain structure.

According to recent reports, participants were from the CARDIA (Coronary Artery Risk Development in Young Adults) study, followed for 30 years, who completed ≥1 cognitive test at year 30. Among participants without diabetes with ≥3 FBG measurements from baseline to year 30, we identified FBG trajectories using latent growth mixture models. Participants who developed diabetes after baseline were included for comparison (n=345). Cognition was assessed using tests of processing speed, executive function, memory, fluency, and global cognition. Structural magnetic resonance imaging data from 605 participants included total gray matter volume and white matter lesions. Associations were examined using multivariable linear regression adjusted for demographics and health behaviors.

Sources indicate that we included 2808 participants (mean age, 55.2±3.6 years; 56% women; 44% Black individuals). Three FBG trajectories were identified: lower‐stable (n=1387), moderate‐stable (n=938), and increasing (n=138). Compared with the lower‐stable group, increasing FBG and incident diabetes were associated with worse performance in memory, processing speed, executive function, and composite cognition; increasing FBG was also associated with worse global cognition. Incident diabetes was associated with lower total and parietal gray matter volume and greater parietal white matter abnormalities. No consistent sex or race interactions were observed.

Persistently elevated glucose below the diabetes threshold was associated with worse cognitive performance in midlife, while incident diabetes was associated with structural brain changes.

What Does Gen Z Think About Political Polarization?

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that polarization is a fact of political life in the U.S.
  • In a recent development, “Polarization doesn’t seem to be a fixed trend in Gen Z’s minds,” stated Jadon Urogdy.
  • Urogdy and his classmates also found that Gen Z, which is the cohort born between 1997 and 2012 and considered the first true “digital natives,” is more comfortable than their elders in having a political conversation online—findings that suggest they may be more reachable and receptive to online interventions aimed at reducing polarization.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that polarization is a fact of political life in the U.S. today. Gen Z, however, is less inclined than older generations to view it as a permanent fixture in American politics, according to research by students in the Stanford political science course Democracy in the Balance: Polarization and the Road Ahead. Students found that Gen Z is more optimistic than any other age group about the possibility of bridging the political divide in America.

In a recent development, “Polarization doesn’t seem to be a fixed trend in Gen Z’s minds,” stated Jadon Urogdy. “We have a bright future. Our identities and views are still malleable, and that’s exactly why this moment matters so much.”.

Urogdy and his classmates also found that Gen Z, which is the cohort born between 1997 and 2012 and considered the first true “digital natives,” is more comfortable than their elders in having a political conversation online—findings that suggest they may be more reachable and receptive to online interventions aimed at reducing polarization.

Sources indicate that urogdy’s results were among many findings from Democracy in the Balance: Polarization and the Road Ahead, a spring quarter course taught by Ashley Fabrizio, a Stanford alum and head of research at the nonpartisan think tank More in Common. Working with Fabrizio and her team, students created and conducted a nationally representative survey of 1,610 U.S. adults that oversampled Gen Z to provide a more granular look into their political attitudes and opinions.

Sources indicate that fabrizio, who has taught the course for three years, has found that working with students surfaces concerns that standard polling may miss. “If we want to know what Gen Z’s political beliefs and attitudes are, we should let our students, as members of Gen Z, use their intuition to decide what matters in a survey,” Fabrizio explained.

Working in small groups, students were allocated several minutes of survey time to explore topics such as the political influence of online content promoting masculinity—aka the “manosphere”—the religious revival in Gen Z’s lives, and their beliefs about the American dream. Fabrizio guided students step by step through survey design, showing them how to craft research questions, field the survey, analyze data, and, finally, present their findings.

Students also examined the academic literature on polarization’s effects in American politics, such as how it contributes to political gridlock, drives support for political violence, and erodes trust in American institutions.

In a recent development, “There are many legitimate divisions in politics over competing policies and values, but polarization often drives us apart unnecessarily,” remarked Fabrizio. “Young Americans will have to find their own ways of bridging partisan differences and overcoming misconceptions about one another. I hope this class helps students see the value of doing so and gives them a sense of agency in addressing polarization.”.

Natalia Galperin was excited about the opportunity to run her own study from start to finish, a first for the Stanford undergrad majoring in psychology. She also wanted to expand on her prior work as a research assistant for political scientist Shanto Iyengar in his Political Communication Lab, where she studied the effects of negative political campaign ads.

For her research project, Galperin examined the role of social media in inflating Gen Z’s hostility toward people from the opposing political party, a phenomenon political scientists call “affective polarization.”.

“We thought Gen Z would be more polarized and misinformed because we get so much of our news on social media compared to older generations,” Galperin noted.

What she and her classmates found reveals a more complicated picture.

While Gen Z respondents who remarked they used social media daily or almost daily were more likely to dislike the opposing party, their scores were almost identical to those of other generations.

“We found that greater social media engagement is generally linked to more polarized views of political parties, and the effect is seen at similar rates across all generations, not just Gen Z,” said Galperin, who will be interning with More In Common this summer.

Practices to help campus communities connect across lines of race, faith, ideology, and more.

Galperin also wanted to know whether social media deepens the divide between what Gen Z thinks people from the other side believe versus what they actually think, a phenomenon known as “perception gaps.” In testing people’s perceptions on immigration, she found that Gen Z did not appear to hold wildly distorted views about the other side—findings that push back against the familiar narrative that being online warps a person’s perceptions of politics.

Taken together, actively using social media seems to harden Gen Z’s feelings more than it distorts basic facts.

The class also found a wide range of political viewpoints, including differences between Gen Z who identified as Democrats and Republicans.

For example, in Urogdy’s project, he and his teammates found that those who were the most confident that polarization can be reduced identified as conservatives and Republicans, while liberals and Democrats believed the opposite—a finding that Urogdy said tracks with prior research: A person’s view of government depends on whether or not their political party is in control.

Galperin’s team also found lower levels of affective polarization among Republicans and Gen Z overall, and Democrats who reported actively using social media daily have higher perception gaps on immigration-related issues than average.

Sources indicate that another student team’s project revealed further complexities. They found that many Gen Z respondents are more likely than other generations to attribute problems like the affordability crisis to systemic failures in democracy itself rather than to specific policies or leaders. In their data, a notable share of young people said the system itself “is not capable of doing its job,” signaling a deeper, structural disillusionment.

“I think we’re all exhausted by the political system,” Urogdy mentioned. “There’s this underlying feeling that what we want isn’t being translated into tangible change, and I think that there’s this overall feeling that instead of having animosity towards people across the aisle, there’s an animosity towards the system itself.”.

Urogdy is pragmatic about what comes next.

Recent findings suggest that “We can’t say polarization will disappear if we will it away,” said Urogdy, who is majoring in political science. Now, he feels he has a better understanding of what kinds of solutions matter. If people are disillusioned with the system, surface-level fixes—such as messaging—won’t last, he said. Efforts need to be ongoing. “If Gen Z is still one of the most reachable generations, the answer is sustained civic engagement, where we can rebuild trust in the system while working to reform it. We have a long path ahead,” said Urogdy, who said he is optimistic.

Fabrizio, too, is hopeful. “Gen Z is inheriting a polarized nation, but they are inheriting deep wells of democratic vitality, as well,” Fabrizio remarked. “America has a long history of self-government, a robust civil society, and communities that remain deeply committed to democratic values. Gen Z has high standards for our democracy, but living up to them is within reach. I hope older generations will listen and be inspired by Gen Z’s vision for the American dream.”.

She attained an M.A. in Media, Culture, & Communication from NYU and a B.Sc. in Sociology from LSE. She was previously the digital communications manager for the Division of Social Sciences at UC Santa Cruz.

Latest Update: Why some people escape Alzheimer’s despite carrying a high-risk gene

📅 19 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1468 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Some people carry one of the strongest genetic risk factors for Alzheimer's disease yet never develop it, remaining mentally sharp well into their 80s.
  • Now, researchers at Columbia University have uncovered a biological mechanism that could help explain this remarkable resistance.
  • It has been revealed that the discovery builds on research the team published two years ago involving APOE ε4, a gene variant strongly associated with Alzheimer's risk.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Some people carry one of the strongest genetic risk factors for Alzheimer's disease yet never develop it, remaining mentally sharp well into their 80s. For years, scientists have wondered what protects these individuals despite their increased genetic vulnerability.

Now, researchers at Columbia University have uncovered a biological mechanism that could help explain this remarkable resistance. Their findings point to a rare genetic mutation that protects the brain's blood vessels from damage, potentially opening a latest path toward Alzheimer's treatments.

It has been revealed that the discovery builds on research the team published two years ago involving APOE ε4, a gene variant strongly associated with Alzheimer's risk. The scientists found that some people carrying APOE ε4 also possess a rare protective mutation in the fibronectin (FN1) gene.

Recent findings suggest that fibronectin is a protein that helps support the structure of tissues. However, in people with APOE ε4, excessive amounts can accumulate around blood vessels in the brain, potentially compromising a critical protective system known as the blood-brain barrier. The rare FN1 mutation appears to limit this buildup and the damage associated with it.

That earlier discovery suggested an intriguing possibility: What if scientists could develop a treatment that recreates the protection provided by this rare mutation?

A new study published in Nature Aging brings that possibility closer by identifying how excess fibronectin damages the brain's protective barrier and revealing potential ways to interrupt the process.

"This fresh study takes us from a genetic clue to a disease mechanism," states Caghan Kizil, the study's corresponding author and professor of neurological sciences in the Department of Neurology and the Taub Institute for Research on Alzheimer's Disease and the Aging Brain at Columbia University Vagelos College of Physicians and Surgeons.

"We knew that changes in fibronectin could protect against Alzheimer's, but we didn't know why excess fibronectin was harmful in the first place. This study gives us that detailed mechanism -- and with it, ideas for how to reproduce that natural protection.".

How an Alzheimer's Risk Gene Weakens the Blood-Brain Barrier.

Industry observers note that the blood-brain barrier serves as a protective boundary between the bloodstream and the brain. Made up of tightly connected cells surrounding the brain's blood vessels, it carefully regulates which substances can enter brain tissue while helping maintain conditions necessary for removing potentially harmful waste.

When this barrier becomes damaged or excessively permeable, substances that would normally be kept out can enter the brain more easily. Such disruptions may contribute to inflammation and other processes involved in neurological diseases, including Alzheimer's.

To investigate the role of fibronectin, the Columbia team combined several advanced research approaches. They examined human brain tissue and cerebrospinal fluid, the clear liquid surrounding the brain and spinal cord, using genetic and epigenetic analyses to explore changes in DNA and gene activity.

Their investigation also included single-cell sequencing, which reveals the activity of individual cells, and spatial imaging to examine where biological changes occur within tissues. Additional experiments involved human stem-cell models, three-dimensional cultures of blood vessels, and studies in zebrafish and mice.

Despite the variety of methods, the findings consistently pointed to the same mechanism: APOE ε4 promotes the production and accumulation of fibronectin around the brain's blood vessels.

Sources indicate that in mice engineered to carry human APOE ε4, researchers measured nearly twice as much fibronectin in the brain as in mice carrying APOE ε3, another common version of the gene. The greater accumulation was accompanied by evidence that the blood-brain barrier had become leaky.

Scientists Discover How Fibronectin Causes Brain Damage.

One experiment provided especially crucial evidence that fibronectin does more than simply accumulate in damaged blood vessels.

The researchers increased human fibronectin specifically in astrocytes, specialized support cells that help maintain the blood-brain barrier and keep the brain functioning properly.

It has been revealed that increasing fibronectin in these cells was enough to disrupt the barrier, allowing it to become more permeable. Conversely, reducing fibronectin improved the barrier's ability to function normally.

These results provided experimental evidence that excess fibronectin can directly contribute to blood-brain barrier damage rather than merely appearing alongside it.

Sources indicate that "The animal experiments allowed us to move beyond association," claims co-first author Prabesh Bhattarai, an associate research scientist in the Kizil lab. "When we increased fibronectin in astroglia, the barrier became permeable. When we reduced fibronectin, barrier function improved.".

The team then investigated the molecular events responsible for the damage.

They found that excessive fibronectin interferes with communication between cells by activating abnormal signals through integrins, proteins that help cells sense and respond to their surroundings, and an enzyme known as focal adhesion kinase.

These abnormal signals disrupt a network of growth factors called VEGF, HBEGF, and IGF1. Although growth factors are often associated with cell development and repair, these particular signaling molecules also help astrocytes and blood vessel cells coordinate their activities to maintain a healthy blood-brain barrier.

When their communication becomes disrupted, the barrier can lose its integrity, potentially leaving brain tissue more vulnerable to damage.

"Single-cell analysis allowed us to examine this pathway in the different cells that maintain the brain's blood vessels," notes co-first author Elanur Yilmaz, an associate research scientist in the Kizil lab. "We observed the same biological pattern across experimental models and human Alzheimer's tissue, making the mechanism especially compelling.".

Evidence From Human Brains Strengthens the Alzheimer's Connection.

Importantly, the researchers found signs of similar biological disturbances in human samples, suggesting that the process identified in laboratory experiments may also contribute to Alzheimer's disease in people carrying APOE ε4.

Analyses of brain tissue and cerebrospinal fluid demonstrated that elevated fibronectin levels were associated with inflammation in astrocytes.

Genetic and gene-regulation analyses also connected FN1 to blood vessel disease and changes involving VEGFA, a growth factor that plays an important role in maintaining healthy brain blood vessels.

Together, these findings provide multiple lines of evidence linking excess fibronectin to the vascular damage associated with APOE ε4.

"The convergence of these independent human datasets strengthens the case that fibronectin is part of the APOE ε4-related vascular disease process," says Badri Vardarajan, associate professor of neurological science in the Department of Neurology, Gertrude H. Sergievsky Center, and Taub Institute, who collaborated on this discovery of the FN1 mutation.

A Rare Genetic Defense Could Inspire Latest Alzheimer's Treatments.

Recent findings suggest that the potential implications are significant because APOE ε4 is the strongest common genetic risk factor for Alzheimer's disease. Approximately one in five people carries at least one copy of this gene variant.

Although carrying APOE ε4 does not guarantee that someone will develop Alzheimer's, it increases their likelihood of developing the disease. Understanding why certain carriers remain unaffected could reveal newly introduced opportunities for prevention and treatment.

The latest findings suggest several possible approaches.

Industry observers note that one strategy would be to prevent harmful amounts of fibronectin from accumulating around the brain's blood vessels. Another would involve blocking the abnormal cellular signals triggered by excess fibronectin. A third possibility would be to restore the growth factor signaling that allows astrocytes and blood vessel cells to maintain the blood-brain barrier.

Researchers are already investigating these possibilities through laboratory experiments.

It has been revealed that however, translating the discovery into a treatment will require considerable care. Fibronectin performs essential functions throughout the body, including supporting tissue structure and helping damaged tissues heal. Any future therapy would therefore need to target its harmful accumulation or effects without disrupting these beneficial activities.

Sources indicate that by identifying the molecular mechanisms involved, scientists now have a more precise framework for designing such treatments. The findings may also help researchers determine when interventions would be most effective and how to measure whether they are successfully protecting the brain.

"By showing how fibronectin contributes to early vascular damage, this study gives us new therapeutic targets and potential ways to measure whether treatments are working," says Richard Mayeux, chair of the Department of Neurology and a collaborator on the project. "Clinically, it connects a major genetic risk factor for Alzheimer's to an early disease process that may be possible to modify.".

Although these potential therapies remain experimental, the discovery offers a promising new direction in Alzheimer's research. Rather than focusing only on the damage that develops as the disease progresses, scientists may eventually be able to reproduce a natural genetic defense that helps protect vulnerable brains before significant damage occurs.

Do art fairs care about non-VIP visitors?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1410 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that october’s Paris art week had become the must-attend fixture of the international art market calendar, particularly for wealthy Americans.
  • Industry observers note that “It’s important to be in Paris,” remarked Chris Sharp, the Los Angeles gallerist and founder of Post-Fair, a boutique California-based event that held its first edition in the French capital this October.
  • The previous weekend, Paris had been rocked by mass demonstrations that in some areas had escalated into riots and looting.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that october’s Paris art week had become the must-attend fixture of the international art market calendar, particularly for wealthy Americans. No other city could match the range and quality of the French capital’s art fairs and exhibitions, both at public museums and private foundations. And what about all those charming restaurants, cafes and shops?

Industry observers note that “It’s important to be in Paris,” remarked Chris Sharp, the Los Angeles gallerist and founder of Post-Fair, a boutique California-based event that held its first edition in the French capital this October. “Paris is the undisputed capital of the art world—once a year,” Sharp added, speaking at Post-Fair’s preview on 19 October, in the chic Marais district. Nearby, someone had sprayed “mort aux riches” across the window of a bank.

The previous weekend, Paris had been rocked by mass demonstrations that in some areas had escalated into riots and looting. Further demonstrations, highlighting the neglected state of France’s secondary schools, the ever-rising cost of living and other grievances, had been planned in Paris and other French cities on the afternoon of Saturday 24 October. Unemployment in France for those aged 15 to 24 at the moment stands at 21.5%, almost three times the rate in neighbouring Germany.

On Tuesday 20 October, the day of the ultra-exclusive Avant-Première pre-preview of Art Basel Paris in the Grand Palais, the French activist collective Pillage de Classe (class plunder) posted a message on Instagram exhorting protesters to “take back” the famous Belle Époque exhibition hall on Saturday, the penultimate day of the week’s flagship fair.

Art Basel Paris has been held in the historic Grand Palais since 2024.

According to recent reports, of course, the Grand Palais was not stormed, Bastille-style. In the highly unlikely event of protesters managing to “take back” the building, they would have been disappointed, just as revolutionaries had been in 1789, when they discovered the prison they had liberated contained just seven detainees. Art Basel Paris, taking no risks, had closed the event two days early on Friday evening (after an excoriating letter from France's gallery association to fair director Karim Crippa, Art Basel recompensed exhibitors 20% of their stand fees).

It has been revealed that the mega-gallery Hauser & Wirth took even fewer risks, emptying its stand the day before, leaving three paintings by the local artist Hélène Delprat. The fair had been shortened to three VIP preview days plus just one day for the general public. Satellite fairs, like Paris Internationale and Post-Fair, closed at lunchtime on Saturday.

That Saturday afternoon, more than 100,000 people duly turned out to demonstrate. However, these proved predominantly peaceful and were confined by the police to the outskirts of the city.

The disruption in Paris had surely been a momentary blip. And Art Basel’s ultra-wealthy invitees, which the top end of the international art trade likes to call the “right kind of people”, had already been and gone. But what about the reputational impact?

“The collateral damage is substantial considering the whole point of being in Paris is to let yourself surrender to its myriad charms,” stated Andrew Terner, a New York-based private dealer and collector, speaking in the immediate aftermath of the early closure.

According to recent reports, the French authorities blamed “ultra-left radical groups” for the violence that had marred weeks of otherwise peaceful protests, begun in September by discontented teenage lycée students. Pillage de Classe is certainly a left-wing radical group; it views Art Basel Paris as a luxury playground in which art is used by the ultra-wealthy to protect their capital from taxation.

But maybe (leaving aside its desire to take the Grand Palais by storm) Pillage de Classe has a point, at least with regard to the fair’s top French clients. In France, the net worth of the country’s 500 wealthiest individuals has ballooned from 6% of the country’s GDP in 1996 to 42% in 2024, according to a much-cited article in the French business magazine Challenges. Tax reforms introduced by President Macron in 2017 excluded stocks, financial assets (including art) and corporate investments from wealth tax calculations.

Moreover, in 2003 the French government had granted tax breaks of up to 75% for private individuals and 60% for corporations that supported the arts. This encouraged investment in glitzy private foundations, such as the Fondation Louis Vuitton, François Pinault’s Bourse de Commerce, the Fondation Cartier and the newly opened Île Seguin luxury hotel and Large art centre, which have become such an alluring feature of the Paris art scene for international visitors. According to research by Apollo magazine, Bernard Arnault’s LVMH luxury group received an aggregate tax break of €518.1m between 2007 and 2017 to set against the €790m the corporation spent building the Frank Gehry-designed Fondation Louis Vuitton.

Recent findings suggest that the ultra-wealthy have also grown a lot wealthier in the US in recent years. The share of the nation’s wealth held by the richest 0.0001% (around 200 individuals) is now more than seven times what it was in 1980, according to a November Substack posted by the Nobel Prize-winning economist Paul Krugman.

Industry observers note that today’s art market is dominated by the world’s wealthiest people buying the world’s most expensive art. Most of these people are pretty old. This is not a good look now that the Democrats have won a landslide victory in the US midterm elections, driven by a massive turnout of young voters. Authoritarian rulers like Viktor Orbán in Hungary and Aleksandar Vučić in Serbia have been voted out of office. Young people have been protesting en masse about their diminished life chances in France and more than a dozen other countries across the world.

Suddenly, ordinary people matter again. The young matter. But do they matter at art fairs?

Take ticket-pricing. In October, the general public were charged £48 each to attend Frieze London, with students being asked to pay £32. Does Frieze, which is owned by the billionaire Ari Emanuel, the former chief executive of the US entertainment conglomerate Endeavor, want to actively discourage young people from visiting? Or is that ticket price an acknowledgement that pretty much the only students who can now afford to attend the UK’s art colleges come from more affluent backgrounds?

Recent findings suggest that the following week, Art Basel Paris, part of James Murdoch’s Lupa Systems investment portfolio, was charging €47 for a standard day pass and €30 for a student ticket. “The galleries pay for the fair. Visitors are a side business,” indicates Magnus Resch, a Upcoming York-based author and art market entrepreneur. According to Resch’s back-of-an-envelope calculations, stand fees generate at least €15m, while tickets bring in less than €3m. “Charging the public €47 isn’t about the money. It’s about keeping the fair exclusive.” (Art Basel does not reveal detailed breakdowns of its revenue streams.).

“It is important for the public to visit an art fair,” says Guillaume Sultana, whose contemporary art gallery exhibited on the upper level of Art Basel Paris, where footfall is slower than down on the ground floor among the mega-galleries. “But a lot of general visitors on the weekend are a bit frustrated because public tickets are very expensive.”.

Sultana acknowledges that “the main business is done during the very first days of an art fair, always”. Despite the fair being truncated, Sultana describes the experience as “very good”, having sold a painting by the young Syrian artist Osama Al Rayyan during the preview for €15,000, among other works.

It has been revealed that in the funfair-mirror optics of the international art market, €15,000 might appear a relatively “affordable” price point. But traditionally, sensible collectors have been advised to spend no more than 5% of their available wealth on art. So, whoever bought that Al Rayan painting, should, theoretically, have had €300,000 of spare cash available. For would-be younger collectors in today’s tough economic conditions, these are intimidating figures, unless they can call on the bank of mum and dad.

Collecting art is in serious danger of being perceived as something that old, rich people do. With so many established collectors ageing and selling, rather than buying, and a democratic wave pushing back against oligarchical wealth, this might be a good moment for the art market to think more about inclusivity than exclusivity, to take a broader view of who might be the “right kind” of people.

After all, who wants “death to the rich” sprayed across their gallery window?
